Examination – General: *Temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, mental status, skin colour, jaundice, lymphadenopathy, rash, petechiae?* — Fever, tachycardia, hypotension = systemic inflammatory response; rash/petechiae may indicate meningococcemia or drug reaction.
Systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) criteria: Fever/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, leukocytosis/leukopenia.
Sepsis and Septic Shock: Severe infections can trigger a systemic inflammatory response.

qs.q: Which of the following findings is a component of the Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) criteria?
o: Serum lactate greater than 2 mmol per liter
Platelet count less than 100,000 per microliter
Heart rate higher than 90 beats per minute
qs.e: SIRS criteria include a heart rate higher than 90/min, alongside temperature extremes, abnormal hyperventilation, and abnormal white blood cell counts. Hypotension and lactate are part of shock or organ dysfunction definitions.

qs.q: Which clinical finding is part of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria?
o: Platelet count lower than 100,000 cells per microliter
Respiratory rate greater than 25 breaths per minute
Body temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C
Systolic blood pressure less than 100 mm Hg
qs.e: SIRS criteria include body temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C, along with heart rate, respiration, and WBC abnormalities. Blood pressure thresholds are not part of the standard SIRS definition.

es.q: Define Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) and list its clinical criteria according to the provided study notes.
es.m:
- **Definition**: SIRS is an exaggerated defense response of the body to a noxious stressor such as infection, trauma, surgery, acute inflammation, ischemia, reperfusion, or malignancy.
- **Body Temperature**: Temperature higher than 38°C or lower than 36°C.
- **Heart Rate**: Heart rate higher than 90 beats per minute.
- **Hyperventilation**: Respiratory rate higher than 20 breaths per minute or PaCO2 lower than 32 mmHg.
- **White Blood Cell Count**: WBC count greater than 12,000 cells/μl or lower than 4,000 cells/μl.
- **Clinical Threshold**: SIRS is considered present when patients have more than one of these clinical findings.

ai.title: Systemic Inflammatory Response
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A clinical syndrome of organ dysfunction triggered by infection or non‑infectious insults. Recognise it early, treat the cause, and support organ systems to prevent shock.

sections.p: Systemic Inflammatory Response is defined by two or more of the following: temperature >38°C or <36°C, heart rate >90/min, respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg, white cell count >12 000/µL, <4 000/µL, or >10% immature neutrophils.
b: Requires at least two criteria to be met
Does not distinguish infection from other causes

t.b: Assess white cell count and differential – leukocytosis or leukopenia with left shift indicates systemic inflammation
Elevated CRP supports ongoing inflammation but is non‑specific
Identify bacterial source; negative cultures do not exclude SIRS
Rule out pneumonia or pleural effusion as infection source

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score. A score ≥2 in any organ system suggests significant organ dysfunction.
b: SOFA includes respiratory, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, CNS, renal parameters

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate: malaria, typhoid, tuberculosis, bacterial meningitis, septicemia from HIV‑related infections, and schistosomiasis. Non‑infectious causes include severe trauma, burns, pancreatitis, and drug reactions.
Patients may appear febrile, tachycardic, tachypnoeic, hypotensive, and confused. Skin may be warm, mottled, or petechial. Respiratory distress and oliguria are common signs of organ compromise.
Prioritise bedside tests; send samples for culture and basic biochemistry. When advanced tests are unavailable, clinical judgment and simple markers guide management.

t.b: Detect malaria parasites or schistocytes in severe infections
Identify proteinuria or haematuria indicating renal involvement
Assess renal function; rising levels predict acute kidney injury
Elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) signals tissue hypoxia and predicts mortality

sections.p: Severe hypotension, persistent tachycardia, oliguria, altered consciousness, and rising lactate are red flags for septic shock and multi‑organ failure.

Treat the underlying cause first (antibiotics, antimalarials, antitubercular therapy). Support organ systems with fluids, vasopressors, oxygen, and renal replacement if needed. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and monitor for bleeding.
Monitor vital signs, organ function, and laboratory markers daily. Prevent recurrence by treating infections early, improving sanitation, and ensuring vaccination coverage.
b: Prompt treatment of urinary tract infections

sections.p: SIRS can mimic non‑infectious inflammatory conditions such as pancreatitis, autoimmune flare, or severe trauma. Distinguish by identifying the source and using specific markers.
In malaria, parasitemia may be low yet severe inflammation persists. In HIV, CD4 counts can be normal despite high viral load. CRP may be normal in early sepsis.

faq.q: Why is a temperature of 36°C considered abnormal in SIRS?
faq.a: Both fever >38°C and hypothermia <36°C are criteria because hypothermia indicates severe systemic inflammation and poorer prognosis.

faq.q: What is the first drug to give in suspected bacterial sepsis in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: A broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotic such as ceftriaxone or ampicillin plus gentamicin, chosen for coverage of common gram‑negative and gram‑positive organisms.

faq.q: How do you manage a patient with SIRS but no obvious source?
faq.a: Obtain cultures, start empiric antibiotics, give fluids, monitor organ function, and repeat investigations to locate the source.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with fever, tachycardia, and oliguria. What is the next best step? — Obtain blood cultures, start empiric antibiotics, and give IV fluids to prevent shock.
In a patient with SIRS, which organ dysfunction score predicts mortality? — SOFA score ≥2 in any system.
A patient with SIRS has a lactate of 3.5 mmol/L. What does this indicate? — Tissue hypoxia and higher mortality risk, prompting aggressive resuscitation.
Which of the following is NOT a SIRS criterion? — Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) is not a criterion.
When should norepinephrine be started in septic shock? — When MAP <65 mmHg despite adequate fluid resuscitation.
Why is a low white cell count still compatible with SIRS? — Leukopenia (<4 000/µL) is one of the criteria, reflecting severe systemic inflammation.
